scenes.title: 보상을 받으면 무엇이 달라질까?
lines: Hello, this is Yamyam Coding.
Have you ever wanted a new character or a piece of music even though it would not raise your attack power?
We will start with rewards that make you stronger, then look at unlocks and collectibles in Super Smash Bros., and finally a checklist that shows what to try next.
By the end, you will be able to describe what one reward changes, the condition for earning it, and the work needed to create it.

scenes.title: 강화와 새로운 능력
lines: The most familiar change is becoming stronger.
You might buy equipment, gain experience and level up, or learn a new skill.
Items from chests and equipment crafted from collected materials fit this pattern too.
For an illustrative example, suppose attack power rises from 10 to 12.
The increase is 2, which is 20 percent of the original value of 10.
That does not mean the actual damage always rises by 20 percent.
Enemy defense and the game's damage formula may also affect the result.
A reward can change an action instead of a number.
Kirby's Copy Abilities change the attacks available to him.
Here he inhales an enemy, gains its ability, and the display changes from Normal to Beam.
A different enemy then gives him Fire, allowing him to breathe flames.
Even without a rising number, players can look forward to what they can do next.
In Bomberman, the possibility of losing the power you have earned also creates tension.
We can explain that relationship with a simple state diagram.
The state before a power-up, the powered-up state, and the state after failure differ, giving players a reason to protect what they have.
But the same approach does not suit every game in the same way.

scenes.title: 대전 전에 모두 육성해야 한다면
lines: What if you want to start a match with a friend right away?
If you first had to spend a long time training the character you wanted to use, you would have preparation to do before the fight.

In Super Smash Bros., a fighter is a combat character you select and control. Making cumulative training a requirement could conflict with a game built around choosing different fighters and competing.
This does not mean no mode in Smash Bros. has power growth.
Separate rules, including the Spirits system we will discuss later, do include it.
We are comparing mandatory training before starting ordinary battles.
To reward play without increasing that burden, we need a change other than higher stats.

scenes.title: 능력치 대신 선택지를 열기
lines: The reward here is a new fighter instead of more attack power.
Unlocking opens a previously locked item. Once the condition is met, it becomes available to use.
In Super Smash Bros. Brawl, a new challenger appears, and defeating that fighter makes them selectable.
Here Toon Link is the challenger.
After winning, we can see the notice that he has joined and his new entry on the selection screen.
Rather than endlessly increasing a number, players gain another set of moves and another way to fight.
Keeping a character locked is also a restriction.
Sakurai says challengers were designed to appear relatively often.
The design balances waiting with the excitement of meeting someone new.
Rescuing a fighter in Ultimate's World of Light uses a different route.
You approach a target on the map, fight, and recruit the fighter after winning.
We should not treat that as the same condition as a challenger appearing or purchasing downloadable content.
After opening new playable options, another kind of reward remains.
It is the pleasure of collecting and looking closely.

scenes.title: 수집할 대상에도 제작 비용이 든다
lines: The collectible figures appearing from Super Smash Bros. Melee through the Nintendo 3DS and Wii U games let players collect and examine characters.
The English menus call them Trophies.
Completing Classic Mode in Melee presents the fighter you just used as a trophy.
Beyond counting how many you own, models and descriptions can introduce characters from other games.
Yet a small collectible for a player can represent many tasks for its developers.
They need to create or adapt a model, build its display interface, prepare descriptive text, and check the result.
Sakurai also describes the burden of producing these trophies.
More rewards mean more of this work.
Can we retain the pleasure of collecting while reducing the work that each item requires?

scenes.title: 스티커에서 스피릿까지
lines: Stickers in Super Smash Bros. Brawl let players collect pictures.
They can represent many characters without all the work of a three-dimensional trophy. In The Subspace Emissary, attached stickers also contribute to power-ups.
This does not mean stickers cost nothing to make.
Preparing images, setting effects, building interfaces, and checking them still take work.
In an illustrative plan, 10 new collectibles taking two hours each require 20 hours.
Add six hours for the common interface and three hours of separate review, and the total is 29 hours.
Total time is item count times work per item, plus shared work and review.
In a real project, items can take different amounts of time, so calculate and add their individual costs.
Ultimate's Spirits develop picture-based collecting into another structure.
It also connects to the fiction of characters who have lost their physical forms.
Primary Spirits provide the basis for attack and defense. Support Spirits fit into slots, the available attachment spaces on a Primary Spirit, to add skills.
On screen, placing the newly acquired Spirit into an empty support slot displays the Unira Equipped skill. It means starting the battle with a spiky ball item called an Unira.
In the following battle, Kirby visibly starts with that item.
Choosing effects and collecting characters meet in one system.
These power-up rules should not be confused with ordinary battles that do not use Spirits.

scenes.title: 모은 코인에는 쓸 곳이 필요하다
lines: Instead of awarding a collectible directly, a game can give coins used to obtain other rewards.
What matters is where you can spend them, not just that a number increases.
In Brawl's Coin Launcher, saved coins are fired as projectiles.
Hitting moving trophies earns them, while defeating groups of small enemies can yield stickers or bonuses.
Holding coins leads to an action and then a collection result.
Calling these coins money for buying ordinary fighters' equipment would describe a different system.
We need to identify the balance, the spending action, and the result separately.

scenes.title: 음악을 보상으로 주면 생기는 두 효과
lines: A reward can also be something to enjoy watching or listening to.
Brawl's earlier results included a notice awarding music.
That track's condition was completing Classic Mode on Normal difficulty, not defeating Toon Link.
Even when rewards appear on the same results sequence, their conditions can differ.
Games can award new music or let players revisit content through music and movie menus.
More music expands what you can hear or select.
But the pleasure of unlocking has another side.
Before the unlock, that content is unavailable.
Keeping a favorite track locked for a long time may create anticipation for one person and an obstacle for another.
Sakurai explains that such inconvenience led later games to rely less on music as an unlockable reward.
That is why we should plan both what to lock and what to provide from the start.
Features such as adjusting menu-music frequencies after completing a particular mode, or revisiting movies already seen, can also be rewards.
Once these different rewards are ready, players need to understand what to do to earn them.

scenes.title: 과제판은 다음 행동을 알려 준다
lines: A checklist makes those conditions visible together.
In Kirby Air Ride, Sakurai included a board resembling the achievement systems that later became familiar on consoles.
Its Japanese name is Clear Getter; the English menu calls it Checklist.
Meeting a condition opens a cell, and hints in nearby cells suggest the next goal.
The connection between conditions and rewards is also visible in the newer Kirby Air Riders.
Here the condition for defeating two cart-riding Waddle Dee enemies at the same time awards a new piece of music and increases the completed total from 47 to 48.
Simply finishing the race is not the condition for this track.
Let us separate the condition and reward using a small illustrative board.
The center cell asks you to finish your first course.
Finishing it marks that cell complete and grants a reward.
A neighboring cell then reveals a hint to collect three coins.
Players can discover something to try without being shown every answer at once.
This is our own example of the relationship between conditions and hints, not a reproduction of the game's interface.
The point is not to fill the screen with boxes.
It is to connect what players have accomplished with what they might try next.

scenes.title: 보상과 요구량을 함께 조절하기
lines: Discovering the next goal does not automatically make its requirement a good one.
Too much repetition for the reward can feel burdensome, while no visible progress can leave players without a reason to continue.
On our board, collecting one coin produces a visible change: one out of three.
Three is not the correct target for every game.
We must consider the time per action, how enjoyable the action is, and the reward's value.
In implementation, it also helps to separate checking the condition from granting the reward.
Record whether the reward has already been granted, so reopening a completed entry does not award it twice.

scenes.title: 보상 한 줄을 먼저 완성하기
lines: Let us return to the opening question.
A reward can be desirable without making us stronger because it offers other kinds of value: a new choice, a collection, something to enjoy, or another goal.
Merely adding item names does not create that value.
For one reward, write down what it changes, how it is earned, the interfaces and materials it needs, and the inconvenience caused while it remains locked.
Then verify that change in actual play.
Doing this early in planning can reduce rushed additions when there is nothing left to award, or promises of more content than the team can finish.
Before deciding how many rewards to make, start with one complete plan that matters to the player and that you can deliver.
